They wanted a partner who could clear up the application’s architecture, make it more stable, and add new features. Someone in the company had already worked with Elinext and knew we had experience with building online payment software. So, we were referred to as a potential partner. We showed our expertise through several related case studies, and the company was convinced we knew what to do and we could execute as much. Process Our collaboration with the client was organized using the outstaffing model. This means we provided a team, and our team worked as a remote part of the client’s organization. We aligned the process with Agile methodology, using Jira to set up a workflow across four development environments with automatic deployments. The work was broken down into five one-week sprints, each of which was built around a particular phase: investigation, implementation, testing, bug fixing and delivery. In large part, the client planned the sprints on their own, consulting our lead developer. And the lead developer was instrumental to monitoring the progress through daily meetings, one with his team and one with the client. In addition to sprints, the entire project included four stages: refactoring, adding new features, developing version 2.0 and improving that version. And the most crucial of them was refactoring. Cleaning The original application we had to work with required quite a few improvements, especially its architecture: we had to rewrite it. We tackled the challenge by using domain-driven design (DDD). This approach allowed us to align the new architecture with the business’ needs and specifics. And the architecture we built as a result proved itself much cleaner, more stable and more load-resilient than the original. Six months from when we hopped on the project, the client had a clean, early version of the application. It included modules and entities that they and prospective businesses using the application could finally comprehend and work with. And no security risks or codebase issues were preventing further development. Taking It to the Next Level Once the application had a clean and efficient architecture, the client green-lighted further improvements. Over the following six months, we added new features and completed the first version of the application as it had been conceived. And we didn’t stop there. It took us one year to build the second version and a year-and-a-half to expand the application, enriching it with further features. Testing Throughout the development, we checked the software using various tests. But end-to-end (E2E) tests played the most important part by allowing us to monitor how new features performed. In the process, we applied a variety of tools to analyze the application and make sure features were delivered in a continuous, timely manner. Product Businesses can use the application to take payments online. Once it has been integrated with a company’s website or mobile app, our client will provide that company with a merchant account and a payment gateway. These will connect the customer’s bank or payment processor with that of the company. We enabled related data storage in DynamoDB, making it compliant with GDPR. The Widget A company can integrate the application with their website or mobile app by installing a widget. The widget supports payments in ten currencies, transferred via commonly used cards (e.g. Mastercard, Visa, Paypal) and custom solutions (e.g. Klarna, SEPA). We also enabled automated recurring payments. The system complies with Payment Card Industry (PCI) standards while not being required to follow the PCI Data Security Standard (DSS). What the widget looks like will depend on the company using it — you can easily customize its appearance. And it’s friendly to users speaking different languages. We set up a localization mechanism that automatically detects the user’s language, and presents the interface in one of ten languages available. We used Native.js with its event system to be managed by an internal state manager (e.g. Redux). This helped prevent potential integration conflicts. The Back End We used Amazon Web Services (AWS) to build the back-end application in the cloud so it can process more than two million requests daily. To streamline transactions, we used a set of technologies. Elastic Load Balancer automatically balances high loads, while Serverless Workflow Orchestrations is responsible for processing transactional mechanisms. Now, if a transaction fails, the payment value will automatically send funds back to the payment card or wallet. Failure reasons may include wrong request handling by third parties, lack of funds in case of automated recurring payments and others. We also applied lambdas for handling scheduled jobs and all possible events. Admin Portal To build the admin portal, we used React.js accompanied by Redux as a state manager and AWS Cognito as an authentication tool. The portal generates access tokens required for integrating the application with a company’s site or mobile app. Portal users can be assigned one of the three roles: Operator, Super Admin and Merchant. A Super Admin manages the application at all levels, assigning user roles, editing organization details, setting up default localizations and more. Operators can create business accounts, generate access tokens and manage a businesses localizations. Finally, Merchant accounts are reserved for businesses. They can manage their business details and use access tokens to integrate the widget with their site or mobile app. Results We completed the project on time, cleaning up the application’s architecture, adding new features and saving the client money by removing third-party tools. And the project overall had been instructive to us, as we improved our understanding of handling huge, highly-loaded payment systems. Today, the product is developing rapidly. And we are preparing for the next stage: refactoring the widget using React Framework.

Msitu Africa is a green fintech company that bridges the gap between businesses and carbon farming projects such as carbon farming and reforestation.The goal is to help digital businesses offset their carbon footprint through our API that automatically collects donations for carbon farming.
reference:
# Msitu Africa: 12-Month Social Media Campaign

**Campaign Theme:** *"Grow Impact With Every Transaction"*
**Core Message:** Msitu Africa connects digital businesses to carbon farming and reforestation projects in Africa. One API integration automatically turns everyday transactions into trees, healthier soil, and measurable climate action.

*(Msitu means "forest" in Swahili.)*

---

## 1. Campaign Foundations

### Goals (12 months)
| Goal | Target |
|---|---|
| Brand awareness | 50K followers across platforms; 1M impressions |
| Lead generation | 500 demo requests from digital businesses |
| Integrations | 50 businesses live on the API |
| Credibility | 10 published impact stories and case studies |

### Target Audiences
1. **Digital business founders and CTOs:** e-commerce, delivery apps, SaaS, fintech, travel and booking platforms
2. **Sustainability and ESG managers** at mid-size companies
3. **Developers**, who often influence tooling decisions
4. **Conscious consumers** who prefer to buy from climate-positive brands
5. **Partners and funders:** NGOs, impact investors, and farming cooperatives

### Platform Strategy
- **LinkedIn:** B2B leads, thought leadership, case studies
- **X (Twitter):** Climate-tech conversations, product updates, developer community
- **Instagram and TikTok:** Storytelling, farmer and field videos, behind-the-scenes
- **YouTube:** API tutorials, documentary-style impact stories
- **Facebook:** Community building and local African business outreach

### Content Pillars
1. **Educate:** carbon footprints, carbon farming, and reforestation explained simply
2. **Show the product:** how the API works, demos, integration steps
3. **Prove impact:** trees planted, farmers supported, CO₂ offset
4. **Inspire:** farmer stories, African climate innovation
5. **Convert:** clear calls to action, offers, partnerships

### Core Hashtags
#MsituAfrica #GrowImpact #GreenFintech #ClimateTech #CarbonFarming #Reforestation #ClimateActionAfrica #SustainableBusiness

---

## 2. Year-at-a-Glance Roadmap

| Phase | Months | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| **Phase 1: Awareness** | 1–3 | Introduce Msitu Africa, the problem, and the solution |
| **Phase 2: Education and Trust** | 4–6 | Explain the tech, show real projects, build credibility |
| **Phase 3: Conversion** | 7–9 | Case studies, partner spotlights, demo drives |
| **Phase 4: Community and Scale** | 10–12 | User-generated content, annual impact report, expansion |

---

## 3. Monthly Plan

### Phase 1: Awareness (Months 1–3)

**Month 1: Launch: "Meet Msitu"**
- Teaser countdown posts (2 weeks before launch)
- Launch video: founder story and the "why"
- Explainer graphic: *Business → API → Carbon Farm → Impact*
- **Hashtag challenge:** #MyBusinessMyForest, where followers share what their business would look like climate-positive
- **CTA:** *Follow us and join the waitlist at [link].*

**Month 2: "The Carbon Problem"**
- Infographic series on digital carbon footprints (servers, deliveries, payments, apps)
- Myth-busting posts: "Offsetting is only for big corporations"
- LinkedIn poll: *Does your business track its carbon footprint?*
- **CTA:** *Calculate your digital footprint with our free tool [link].*

**Month 3: "What Is Carbon Farming?"**
- Short educational reels with farmers and agronomists
- Carousel: 5 ways carbon farming restores African land
- Instagram Live Q&A with the founder
- **CTA:** *Book a free 15-minute demo.*

### Phase 2: Education and Trust (Months 4–6)

**Month 4: "How the API Works"**
- 60-second animated product demo
- Developer-focused thread on X: "Integrate climate action in under an hour"
- YouTube tutorial: step-by-step integration
- **CTA:** *Get your API key and start offsetting today.*

**Month 5: "Meet the Projects"**
- Photo and video series from partner carbon farms and reforestation sites
- Farmer spotlight stories
- Explain verification and transparency: how impact is tracked and reported
- **CTA:** *See where your impact goes: explore our project map.*

**Month 6: "Mid-Year Impact Report"**
- Publish first impact numbers (trees planted, hectares restored, CO₂ offset)
- Behind-the-scenes team content
- Live webinar: *"Making Your Business Climate-Positive Without Slowing Down Growth"*
- **CTA:** *Register for the webinar and get our integration guide.*

### Phase 3: Conversion (Months 7–9)

**Month 7: "Early Adopter Stories"**
- First customer case study (video and written)
- Testimonial quote cards
- Before and after: *"What changed after adding Msitu"*
- **CTA:** *Join our first 50 partner businesses and get a founding-partner badge.*

**Month 8: "Customers Care"**
- Content showing consumers prefer sustainable brands (stats and surveys)
- Co-branded posts with partner businesses: "This purchase planted a tree"
- Marketing toolkit for partners: badges, checkout banners, email templates
- **CTA:** *Show your customers you care: add the Msitu badge to your checkout.*

**Month 9: "Partner Month"**
- Partner spotlight series (one per week)
- Collaboration with African climate influencers and tech communities
- Run a sponsored campaign on LinkedIn targeting e-commerce and fintech founders
- **CTA:** *Become a Msitu partner: start your free pilot.*

### Phase 4: Community and Scale (Months 10–12)

**Month 10: "Grow Together"**
- User-generated content campaign: partners and customers share their "tree moment"
- Community leaderboard: top contributing businesses
- Employee and developer volunteering days on partner farms
- **CTA:** *Tag us in your impact story with #GrowImpact.*

**Month 11: "Climate Action Season"**
- Tie into COP and year-end sustainability conversations
- Giving-season campaign: *"Gift a forest this holiday"* for customers and teams
- Thought-leadership articles on African carbon markets
- **CTA:** *Make your Q4 transactions count: integrate before year-end.*

**Month 12: "Year in Review and What's Next"**
- Annual impact report: video, infographic, and full PDF
- Thank-you posts to farmers, partners, and followers
- Announce year-two goals and new regions or features
- **CTA:** *Read our impact report and join our next chapter.*

---

## 4. Weekly Posting Rhythm

| Day | Content Type |
|---|---|
| Monday | Educational post (carousel or infographic) |
| Tuesday | Product or API tip (short video) |
| Wednesday | Impact story or farmer spotlight |
| Thursday | Engagement post (poll, quiz, Q&A) |
| Friday | Partner or team feature |
| Weekend | Light, inspiring content (nature, reposts, community) |

---

## 5. Ready-to-Share Sample Posts

### LinkedIn Launch Post
> 🌍 What if every transaction on your platform helped grow a forest?
>
> Meet **Msitu Africa**, a green fintech connecting digital businesses to carbon farming and reforestation projects across Africa.
>
> With one simple API, your business can automatically collect contributions at checkout and fund verified projects that restore land, support farmers, and cut carbon.
>
> ✅ Quick integration
> ✅ Transparent impact tracking
> ✅ Real benefits for African communities
>
> 👉 **Book your free demo today: [link]**
>
> #MsituAfrica #GreenFintech #ClimateTech #GrowImpact

### Instagram/Facebook Caption
> Every click can plant hope. 🌱
> Msitu Africa helps online businesses turn everyday transactions into trees and healthier land, automatically.
>
> 🌳 Add our API
> 🌍 Offset your footprint
> 👩🏾‍🌾 Support African farmers
>
> Ready to grow? Tap the link in bio to get started.
> #MsituAfrica #GrowImpact #ClimateActionAfrica

### X (Twitter) Post
> Your app already processes payments.
> What if it also planted trees? 🌳
>
> Msitu Africa's API automates carbon farming donations, with no heavy lifting for your team.
>
> Start offsetting today 👉 [link]
> #ClimateTech #GreenFintech

### Developer Thread Opener (X)
> 🧵 How to make your product climate-positive in under an hour:
> 1/ Get your Msitu API key
> 2/ Set your contribution rule (per transaction, per order, or a percentage)
> 3/ Go live and watch impact build in real time 🌱

### TikTok/Reels Script (30 sec)
> **Hook:** "This online order just planted a tree. Here's how."
> **Middle:** Show checkout → API icon → farmer planting → impact dashboard.
> **Close:** "Msitu Africa: climate action, built into your business. Link in bio."

---

## 6. Calls to Action (Rotate These)
- **Book a free demo**
- **Get your API key**
- **Calculate your footprint**
- **Become a founding partner**
- **Add the Msitu badge to your checkout**
- **Download the impact report**

---

## 7. Budget Allocation (Suggested)
| Item | Share |
|---|---|
| Video and content production | 30% |
| Paid social ads (LinkedIn, Meta, X) | 30% |
| Influencer and partner collaborations | 15% |
| Events and webinars | 10% |
| Tools (scheduling, analytics, design) | 5% |
| Community and giveaways | 5% |
| Contingency | 5% |

---

## 8. Measurement and KPIs

**Track monthly:**
- Follower growth, reach, and engagement rate
- Click-through rate to website and demo page
- Demo requests and API sign-ups
- Cost per lead
- Number of live integrations
- Impact metrics: trees planted, hectares restored, CO₂ offset
- Sentiment and brand mentions

**Review quarterly:** Double down on top-performing content and adjust messaging for each audience.

---

## 9. Trust and Compliance Tips
- Use verified, third-party-audited data and avoid overstating impact claims (prevents greenwashing).
- Credit farmers and communities respectfully, with consent for photos and stories.
- Be transparent about how contributions are used and what share goes to projects.

---

## 10. Next Steps
1. Finalize your brand kit (logo, colors, tone of voice).
2. Build a landing page with a demo booking form and a footprint calculator.
3. Capture photo and video assets from partner projects.
4. Schedule the first 30 days of content.

1. **"As you know"**：如果这是第一次正式通知，对方未必"已经知道"，显得略突兀。可改为 "We are pleased to inform you that..."。
2. **"To support this project"**：稍显笼统，可以说明培训对供应商的作用。
3. **"designed to introduce"**：可以，但 "designed to introduce you to" 或 "which will introduce" 更顺。
4. **时间信息**：缺少年份、星期和时区，国际邮件中建议补充，避免误解。
5. **"via Teams"**：建议写成 "via Microsoft Teams"，并提示会后将发送链接。

>

>
> The session will be conducted in English and is designed to introduce the Centric Brands Compliance System. The meeting link will be sent separately.
>
> Please let us know if you will be able to attend.
>
> Best regards,
> [Your Name]

> As one of the selected suppliers for the Centric Brands Packaging Optimization Project, your company is invited to a training session on June 8, 9:30–10:30 am, via Microsoft Teams. The session will be conducted in English and will introduce the Centric Brands Compliance System.

# Price Skimming Strategy for Caviish

## 1. Why Price Skimming Fits Caviish

Price skimming means launching at a high price to capture the segment most willing to pay, then adjusting over time. It suits Caviish for these reasons:

| Condition for skimming | How Caviish meets it |
|---|---|
| Unique, non-replicable product | Each item is one-of-a-kind, and its value comes from the celebrity who owned or wore it |
| Price-insensitive early buyers | Top-tier fans and collectors seek exclusivity and status |
| Value driven by perception | The story, the event, authentication, and the fan meeting matter more than the item's retail cost |
| Small catalog, limited volume | 22 products from 10 celebrities. Low volume means premium margins matter |
| Brand positioning | "Luxury experience" is undermined by discounting at launch |
| Commission model (10%) | Higher sale prices raise Caviish's revenue per transaction directly |

**Important caveat:** Classic skimming relies on gradual price reductions. Because each Caviish item is unique, the "reduction" happens through time-based markdowns on unsold items, or through new product tiers, not through mass-market price drops.

## 2. Pricing Framework

### Step 1: Classify each product (using Caviish's four types)

| Category | Skimming intensity | Price logic |
|---|---|---|
| **Luxury, worn at a known event** (e.g., a Rolex worn at a film premiere) | Very high | Retail value + celebrity premium of 3–10x or more, depending on fame and visibility |
| **Luxury, not worn at an event** | Moderate to high | Retail or resale value + a 1.5–3x celebrity premium |
| **Non-luxury, worn at an event** | High | Priced mainly on story and iconic status. The premium can be many times the item's cost |
| **Non-luxury, not worn at an event** | Moderate | Accessible entry-level pricing, with the premium coming from ownership alone |

### Step 2: Calculate the premium with a scoring model

Price = Base value × Celebrity Premium Multiplier

The multiplier is built from weighted factors:
- **Celebrity tier** (Class A global star vs. regional): 30%
- **Visibility of the item** (iconic scene, award show, match): 25%
- **Scarcity and condition** (one-off, signed, limited): 15%
- **Authentication strength** (production house letter, NFT, video): 15%
- **Added experience** (video call, coffee meeting, signed note): 15%

Each factor is scored 1–5, and the total is mapped to a multiplier range. For example, a score of 4.5+ maps to 6–10x.

## 3. The Skimming Timeline

### Phase 1: Premium launch (Weeks 1–4)
- List at full skimming price.
- Target VIP fans, collectors, and followers of that celebrity.
- Offer early access to a "Caviish Insider" list, with a 24–48 hour exclusive window before public release.
- Pair the launch with a marketing moment such as a film release, festival, or tournament.
- Include the full value stack: video clip, NFT, authentication letter, and fan meeting.

### Phase 2: Controlled adjustment (Weeks 5–10)
- If unsold, reduce the price by 10–15%, framed as a "final release window" and not a discount.
- Add value instead of cutting price where possible, such as a handwritten note or an extra video message.
- Retarget engaged visitors, meaning those who viewed or saved the item.

### Phase 3: Broader market (Weeks 11–16)
- Reduce by another 10–20%, or move the item to an auction format, which is already on Caviish's roadmap. Auctions let the market set the price and can exceed the fixed price for hot items.
- Bundle lower-tier items, such as a "Collector's Set" from one celebrity.

### Phase 4: Review and retire
- After about four months, consult the celebrity. Options include relisting with a new story, donating the item to a charity auction, or returning it.
- Never go below the agreed minimum with the celebrity, to protect their reputation.

**Exception:** Highly iconic items should hold their price indefinitely. Discounting a signature piece can damage both the celebrity's and Caviish's brand.

## 4. Protecting the Premium Positioning

Skimming only works if buyers believe the price is justified. Since trust is Caviish's biggest challenge, the strategy depends on:

1. **Authenticity proof:** production house letters, event video, photos of the celebrity wearing the item, and later the NFT.
2. **Storytelling:** each listing should tell where, when, and why the item was worn.
3. **Scarcity signals:** "1 of 1" labels, countdown timers, and a visible "sold" archive showing past prices.
4. **Charity tie-in:** the celebrity's donation of part or all proceeds justifies a higher price emotionally, since buyers are also giving.
5. **Luxury presentation:** premium packaging, a certificate of ownership, and a personalized unboxing.
6. **Social proof:** buyer testimonials, unboxing videos, and celebrity shout-outs.

## 5. Segmentation and Targeting

| Segment | Profile | Approach |
|---|---|---|
| **Super fans / collectors** | High income, emotionally attached | Early access, premium prices, personal experience |
| **Gift buyers** | Buying for a fan or a special occasion | Gift packaging, mid-tier items |
| **Investors / NFT enthusiasts** | Interested in digital and resale value | NFT-linked items, with provenance as the selling point |
| **Gulf and high-income markets** | Strong luxury spending, celebrity culture | Initial focus markets, with Arabic-language campaigns |

## 6. Financial Illustration

| Scenario | Sale price | Caviish 10% commission | Celebrity receives |
|---|---|---|---|
| Penetration price (e.g., $500) | $500 | $50 | $450 |
| Skimming price (e.g., $2,500) | $2,500 | $250 | $2,250 |
| Skimming with a 15% later reduction | $2,125 | $212.50 | $1,912.50 |

Even after a reduction, the skimmed price earns far more per transaction than a low entry price. With only 22 products, this matters more than volume.

## 7. Risks and Mitigation

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Fans don't know the brand, so high prices stall sales | Build trust first through authentication, social proof, and production house partnerships. Use the launch window to generate buzz |
| Price seen as unjustified | Show the value stack clearly and share the story behind the price |
| Unsold items harm perception | Use "final release" framing, auctions, or added value instead of visible cuts |
| Celebrity dissatisfaction if items sell below expectations | Agree on a price floor and the timeline in the contract |
| Competitors or counterfeits | Use NFT authentication and exclusive celebrity contracts |
| Currency differences across Egypt, the Gulf, and the UK | Price in USD or GBP for premium items, and use the London branch for transactions |

## 8. Recommendations

1. **Use a hybrid approach.** Apply skimming to top-tier items, and use moderate pricing for non-luxury or less-famous items to build volume and trust.
2. **Start with 3–5 hero products** from the most famous celebrities, and build campaigns around them.
3. **Test and learn.** With a small catalog, track views, saves, and conversion rates at each price point to refine the multiplier model.
4. **Introduce auctions for the most in-demand items.** They are a natural extension of skimming and can exceed fixed prices.
5. **Consider a price floor agreement** with each celebrity, so adjustments don't conflict with their image.
6. **Reinvest early premium revenue** into marketing and authentication, which in turn supports the premium price.

## 9. Conclusion

Price skimming matches Caviish's one-of-a-kind products, its luxury positioning, and the strong emotional pull of celebrity ownership. Success depends on credibility. Premium prices will work only if fans trust the authenticity and feel the story and experience justify the cost. By starting high with top-tier items, adjusting through time-limited windows and auctions, and reinforcing value through NFTs, production house letters, and charity involvement, Caviish can maximize revenue per transaction while building its reputation as the credible global leader in celebrity belongings.

# Social Innovation: Implementation, Effectiveness and Community Value
### A Case Perspective: Msitu Africa

## 1. What Social Innovation Means

Social innovation refers to new products, services, models, or processes that address social or environmental needs more effectively than existing approaches, while building new relationships and capabilities among the people involved. Msitu Africa fits this definition. It combines climate action, technology, and rural livelihoods in one model, linking corporate carbon-reduction goals directly to smallholder farmers.

## 2. How Social Innovation Can Be Implemented

**a) Identify a clear problem and a target community.**
Msitu Africa addresses two connected problems: businesses lack credible, easy ways to offset emissions, and smallholder farmers lack finance, training, and access to carbon markets.

**b) Build a bridging mechanism.**
Its API automates and simplifies donations, linking corporate contributions to verified farmers and projects. This lowers transaction costs, increases transparency, and makes participation easy for companies of any size.

**c) Invest in capacity building.**
Training in carbon farming, ongoing guidance, and funding mean the community is not just a beneficiary but an active, skilled participant. Innovation that transfers skills tends to last longer than aid that transfers only money.

**d) Create a self-reinforcing income model.**
Farmers gain higher yields and earn revenue from sequestered carbon credits. This gives them a financial reason to maintain trees and soil practices over the long term.

**e) Partner across sectors.**
Implementation depends on collaboration among corporations (funders), farmers (implementers), technology providers, local authorities, and verification bodies.

**f) Measure, learn, and adapt.**
Tracking tree survival, carbon sequestered, farmer income, and corporate participation allows the model to improve and to build credibility.

## 3. Effectiveness

**Environmental:** Tree planting and carbon farming remove CO₂, restore soil, improve water retention, and increase biodiversity.

**Economic:** Farmers gain diversified income through higher yields and carbon credit revenue, which builds resilience against drought and unstable crop prices.

**Scalability:** A digital API lets the model expand across Kenya and other African markets without proportionally increasing administrative costs.

**Trust and accountability:** Direct, traceable links between donors and projects reduce the intermediary leakage and greenwashing concerns that undermine many offset schemes.

**Key risks to manage:**
- Ensuring fair carbon revenue sharing and clear farmer contracts
- Reliable monitoring, reporting, and verification of carbon claims
- Tree survival and permanence over decades
- Avoiding dependence on a few corporate donors
- Farmer digital and financial literacy

## 4. Value to Targeted Communities

- **Income and livelihoods:** New revenue streams and better yields improve household food and financial security.
- **Skills and empowerment:** Technical knowledge stays in the community and can be passed on.
- **Climate resilience:** Healthier soils, shade, and tree cover help farms withstand climate shocks.
- **Inclusion in global markets:** Smallholders, usually excluded from carbon markets, gain access.
- **Community cohesion and ownership:** Collective projects strengthen local networks and give communities a stake in environmental stewardship.
- **Wider benefits:** Cleaner water, restored land, and potential for local green jobs.

## 5. Conclusion

Msitu Africa shows how social innovation works best: it pairs technology with human development, aligns the incentives of businesses and communities, and delivers environmental and economic benefits together. Its long-term effectiveness will depend on transparent benefit-sharing, rigorous verification, and continued community participation in design and decision-making. query: i READ A PARAGRAPH IN "THE POWER LAW" WHICH IS A BOOK ABOUT VENTURE CAPITAL AND RISK INVESTMENT :"As Netscape’s stock climbed further, Kleiner soon found itself sitting on a profit of $500 million: it had achieved a multiple of 100x, or roughly twice as much as Accel’s multiple on UUNET." WHAT IS THE MEANING OF " achieved a multiple of 100x," DOES THAT MEAN 100 TIMES Price–earnings ratio ? Answer me with your knowledge about history
reference:
No, it is not a price-earnings ratio. A "multiple" in venture capital means **multiple on invested capital (MOIC)**, also called a "cash-on-cash return." It is the value of the investment divided by the amount originally put in.

**What "100x" means here**

Kleiner Perkins invested about **$5 million** in Netscape in 1995, at an early stage when the company was young. When Netscape went public in August 1995 and the stock soared, that stake was worth about **$500 million**.

$500 million ÷ $5 million = **100x**

So every dollar Kleiner put in became about one hundred dollars. The "profit of $500 million" in the quote is a rounded, approximate figure. Strictly, the stake's value was about $500 million, and the profit was that minus the initial investment.

**Why it's not P/E**

- **P/E ratio** = share price ÷ earnings per share. It is used in public markets to judge how expensive a stock is relative to its profits. Netscape actually had very little profit at its IPO, so its P/E was nearly meaningless.
- **Investment multiple** = what you got back ÷ what you put in. It measures the investor's return, and it is the standard way VCs describe their wins.

**Historical context**

- Netscape's IPO in August 1995 was a landmark event. The stock was priced at $28, jumped to over $70 on the first day, and helped set off the dot-com boom.
- Kleiner's partner John Doerr led the Netscape investment, and it made his reputation.
- The comparison in the book is with **Accel's investment in UUNET**, an early internet service provider. Accel got roughly a 50x multiple. Kleiner's 100x was "twice as much."

**Why this matters in "The Power Law"**

Sebastian Mallaby's central point is that venture returns follow a power-law distribution. A few huge winners, such as a 100x, generate most of a fund's returns, and they outweigh the many investments that fail or return little. That is why VCs chase rare outsized outcomes instead of steady, moderate gains.

For this we will need the following from your team: 1. Access to the full clinical trial protocol currently being used in India, so we can align our methodologies and ensure consistency in data collection and analysis. 2. Results and data from the bioequivalence studies conducted with your participants, which will serve as a crucial benchmark for our integrated analysis. reference:
I can't give you a protocol or study data, and I should be clear about my role. I'm an AI assistant, not a sponsor, CRO, or research team. I have no access to any Indian clinical trial protocol or participant data. Even if I did, sharing it would require the sponsor's authorization. Please direct this request to the sponsor or CRO that holds the data.

Some points may also help you plan the proposal.

**Regulatory issues with the approach**

1. **Bioequivalence studies and multicenter patient trials are different things.** BE studies for generics are usually small crossover studies in healthy volunteers, or in patients when safety requires it. They are not normally run as patient-recruitment trials across sites. Adding a Russian site for patient recruitment would not replace a BE study unless the design and the regulator's requirements support it.

2. **Pooling data is limited.** Under the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) rules (Decision No. 85 on BE studies) and Russian Ministry of Health requirements, BE data generally need to come from a study that meets those standards. Results from a study already run in India can be accepted only if they meet GCP and the comparator and design requirements, and if the regulator agrees. Merging them with new Russian data into a "combined" analysis is not automatically acceptable and would need a prespecified statistical plan.

3. **Comparator product.** The reference product should be the originator (Doptelet/Doptelet®, Sobi/AkaRx) or one the regulator accepts, and the batch, strength and sourcing need to be documented.

4. **Russian clinical trial approval.** A trial conducted in Russia requires Roszdravnadzor permission, an ethics council opinion, local insurance of participants, and, for international trials, compliance with Federal Law 61-FZ and the EAEU rules. Most of this is needed before enrollment can begin.

5. **Data ownership and confidentiality.** Access to another sponsor's protocol and results needs a contract: a confidentiality agreement, a data-sharing or licensing agreement, and a right-of-reference or similar document. Without this, the data cannot be used in your dossier.

**A practical path**

- Consult a regulatory affairs specialist or CRO with Russian and EAEU experience.
- Request a scientific advice meeting or consultation with Roszdravnadzor and its expert body (FGBU "NCEMP") on whether the Indian study can support registration, and what bridging is required.
- Check whether the Indian study followed ICH-GCP and the EAEU design and sample requirements. If it did, consider a bridging study or a separate small BE study in Russia.
- If you hold the rights to the data, negotiate a data-sharing agreement. If you do not, you need your own study.
- Establish whether avatrombopag fits a biowaiver. This is unlikely given its properties (food effect, and a need for strength proportionality data) and it should be checked against the guidelines.

I can help draft a regulatory strategy outline, a letter requesting scientific advice, a data-sharing term sheet, or a BE study synopsis for avatrombopag. Tell me which you would like.

Bonjour Mounir,

J'espère que vous allez bien.

En réponse à votre email, je vous informe que je n'ai pas effectué de passation de consignes réglementaire avec le RDGN sortant, Monsieur Riadh SHIL, en présence du contrôle de gestion.

- le contrat annuel de CAMPSYSTEM ;
- le contrat annuel de Safran ;
- le contrat des moteurs STD Aero ;
- un fichier relatif aux comptes rendus d'incident matériel ;

- la convention entre TE et TT.

- ni la liste des prélèvements de pièces effectués sur l'avion TS-LBD ;

- « Mais j'ai pas reçu » → « En revanche, je n'ai reçu ni… ni… » (négation correcte).
- « après avoir donner » → formulation corrigée (infinitif erroné).

reference:
# Covid-19 and South Western Railway: Positive and Negative Impacts

I don't have the full text of the case, so this analysis draws on what is publicly known about South Western Railway (SWR, the UK operator) and on general design-thinking logic. Check it against the case facts, and tell me if you meant the Indian Railways zone based in Hubballi.

## Negative impacts

1. **Collapse in demand and revenue.** Lockdowns and remote work cut ridership by roughly 80–95% at the low point. SWR serves a heavily commuter-based market (London Waterloo, Surrey, Hampshire), so it was especially exposed.
2. **Loss of the financial model.** Fare revenue could not cover costs. The government replaced the franchise risk with emergency agreements (from March 2020), which reduced SWR's commercial freedom and made long-term experiments harder to fund.
3. **Disruption of the experimentation process.** Design thinking relies on observing users, prototyping in real settings, and gathering quick feedback. Social distancing, fewer passengers, and staff absences made field tests and ethnographic observation harder, and old baselines became unreliable.
4. **Operational strain.** Staff sickness and shielding forced timetable cuts. Cleaning, signage, and crowd-management requirements added cost and complexity.
5. **Uncertainty about future demand.** Hybrid working changed peak patterns and made season tickets less attractive, so the problems the team had been designing for shifted.
6. **Passenger trust and safety concerns.** Passengers feared crowded, enclosed spaces.

## Positive impacts

1. **Urgency and a license to experiment.** The crisis created permission to try fast, low-cost changes: one-way flow systems, floor markings, and real-time crowding information. Design-thinking approaches (empathize, prototype, test, iterate) fit this setting well.
2. **Sharper focus on user needs.** Safety, cleanliness, flexibility, and information became the central needs, which gave the team clear problems to define.
3. **Digital acceleration.** There was faster adoption of contactless and mobile ticketing, app-based crowding and seat information, and digital communication.
4. **Quieter network as a testbed.** Fewer passengers made it safer and easier to trial layout changes, timetable patterns, and station processes with little risk of major disruption.
5. **Cross-functional collaboration.** Operations, safety, marketing, and frontline staff worked together faster, with fewer hierarchical barriers.
6. **New products and markets.** The shift toward flexible tickets (such as part-time commuter fares) and leisure travel opened new segments.

## Link to design thinking

| Stage | Covid effect |
|---|---|
| Empathize | Harder to observe in person, but needs were clearer (safety, certainty) |
| Define | Problem shifted from "reduce crowding and delays" to "rebuild confidence and flexibility" |
| Ideate | Broader openness to unconventional ideas |
| Prototype/Test | Faster, cheaper trials; but unstable baselines weakened the data |

## Conclusion

Covid-19 hurt SWR financially and operationally and made controlled experimentation harder. It also forced rapid, user-centred innovation, accelerated digital tools, and made experimentation more acceptable inside the organization. The key lesson is that small, fast, low-cost experiments helped manage uncertainty better than large planned programmes.

query: If Jim puts in an order to purchase 30 shares of company A for $1.30 while the current price is $1.35, and the order is canceled immediately, what type of order did he put in? choose from the following: Limit Order Market Order Fill or Kill Order Stop-Loss Order
reference:
The answer is **Fill or Kill Order**.

**Why:**
- A **market order** executes immediately at the current price, so it wouldn't be placed at $1.30 when the price is $1.35.
- A **stop-loss order** is used to sell once a price falls to a certain level, so it doesn't fit a buy order like this.
- A **limit order** sets a maximum buy price of $1.30, but it would normally stay open until the price drops to that level or until Jim cancels it. It would not be canceled immediately.
- A **fill or kill order** must be executed in full immediately, or it is canceled. The market price of $1.35 is above Jim's $1.30 limit, so the order couldn't be filled right away, and it was canceled at once.

**Fill or Kill Order**

The sentence is understandable but has a few grammar and style problems.

**Issues:**
1. "the enclosed email... reply below" is confusing. It's unclear whether you are enclosing an email or quoting a reply.
2. "reply below" needs an article or a possessive ("the reply below").
3. "for your further arrangement" is unidiomatic. "For your further action" or "for further arrangements" is more natural.
4. The supplier's name doesn't need quotation marks or all capitals.

**Suggested revisions:**

- **If the reply is quoted below the message:**
 "Please find below the reply from our supplier, the Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists, for your further action."

- **If the reply is attached:**
 "Please find attached the reply from our supplier, the Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists, for your further action."

- **Slightly more formal:**
 "Please see below the reply from the Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists. Kindly make the necessary arrangements."

Note: "enclosed" is usually used for physical letters or attachments. For text pasted in the body of an email, use "below."

reference:
# NEHEMIAH HOUSE
### A 6-Minute Documentary: Voiceover Script

**Note:** I don't have verified details about Nehemiah House, so anything in [brackets] is a placeholder to replace with confirmed facts: founding date, founder names, program length, statistics, and quotes. Interview slots are marked where real testimonies should go. Narration runs about 700 words, leaving room for interviews and natural sound.

---

## COLD OPEN (0:00–0:30)

**VISUALS:** Pre-dawn Little Rock. Empty streets, a traffic light changing, the Arkansas River in fog. A porch light clicks on at a modest house.

**VO:**
Before the city wakes up, someone here is already awake. Praying. Making coffee. Getting ready for another day of the hardest work they'll ever do.

This is Nehemiah House.

---

## ACT ONE: THE PROBLEM (0:30–1:30)

**VISUALS:** Local street scenes, a shuttered motel, a hospital sign, a newspaper headline about addiction in Arkansas [verify and insert].

**VO:**
Addiction doesn't announce itself. It moves quietly through neighborhoods, through families, through church pews. In Arkansas, thousands of people are fighting a battle with opioids, methamphetamine, and alcohol [insert verified state statistics].

For many, the bottom isn't a single moment. It's a long fall, with relationships, jobs, and hope lost along the way.

**VISUALS:** Hands gripping a table. A phone with unanswered calls. An empty chair at a dinner table.

**VO:**
And for those ready to climb out, the question is often the same: *Where do I even begin?*

---

## ACT TWO: THE NAME AND THE MISSION (1:30–2:30)

**VISUALS:** The exterior of Nehemiah House. A sign. Residents carrying supplies. A hand-painted Bible verse on the wall.

**VO:**
In the Old Testament, Nehemiah was a man who looked at a city in ruins, broken walls and burned gates, and didn't turn away. He picked up a trowel and started to rebuild.

That story shaped everything here.

Nehemiah House was founded in [year] by [founder name(s)], who believed that lives, like cities, can be rebuilt, one stone at a time [adjust to the real origin story].

**VISUALS:** A staff member unlocking the door and greeting a new arrival.

**VO:**
The program is faith-based, rooted in the Christian gospel, and built on structure, accountability, and community. Residents live together for [length of program], sharing meals, chores, counseling, and worship.

---

## ACT THREE: A DAY IN THE HOUSE (2:30–4:00)

**VISUALS:** Morning devotions. Men or women [confirm] sitting in a circle. Breakfast. Work duty. A counseling session through a window. Group Bible study. Afternoon work or vocational training.

**VO:**
The day begins early. Prayer. Scripture. Breakfast together.

Then comes work: cleaning, cooking, maintaining the house [adjust]. It's not busywork. It's the rebuilding of habits that addiction destroyed. Showing up. Finishing what you start. Being someone others can count on.

**INTERVIEW SLOT #1 (≈20 sec): Resident**
*Suggested prompt: "What was your first week like?"*

**VISUALS:** One-on-one counseling. A whiteboard with the day's schedule. Laughter in the kitchen.

**VO:**
There are classes and counseling, and there are hard conversations. But there's also laughter, shared meals, and the quiet discovery that you're not alone.

**INTERVIEW SLOT #2 (≈20 sec): Staff member or director**
*Suggested prompt: "Why does faith matter in recovery?"*

**VO:**
For the people here, recovery isn't just about stopping something. It's about becoming someone.

---

## ACT FOUR: A STORY OF CHANGE (4:00–5:15)

**VISUALS:** A graduate or longer-term resident at work, with family, or at church. Old photos, if they consent.

**VO:**
[Name] arrived at Nehemiah House in [year], after [brief, consented summary of their story].

**INTERVIEW SLOT #3 (≈30–40 sec): Graduate or resident**
*Suggested prompt: "What changed for you here?"*

**VISUALS:** The person walking into a church, hugging a family member, or starting a shift at work.

**VO:**
Not every story ends this way. Recovery is rarely a straight line, and relapse is a reality the staff here know well. But they also know that no one is beyond rebuilding.

That belief is what keeps the lights on.

---

## CLOSING (5:15–6:00)

**VISUALS:** Evening at Nehemiah House. Residents sharing dinner, then a quiet prayer. The porch light glows as the sun sets over Little Rock.

**VO:**
Nehemiah rebuilt a wall in fifty-two days. Here, the work takes longer. It happens in small victories: a sober morning, a phone call to a parent, a prayer whispered at the end of a hard day.

The walls of a life can fall. But in a quiet house in Little Rock, people are picking up the stones and starting again.

**VISUALS:** Fade to the Nehemiah House sign.

**TEXT ON SCREEN:**
*Nehemiah House, Little Rock, Arkansas*
*[Website / phone number / how to help or get help]*
*If you or someone you love is struggling with addiction, call the SAMHSA National Helpline: 1-800-662-4357 (free, confidential, 24/7).*

---

**Production notes:**
- Get signed releases from every resident and graduate featured. Privacy is critical in recovery settings.
- Score suggestion: sparse piano and acoustic guitar, building gently in Act Four.
- Verify the program details, the founding story, and all statistics with Nehemiah House directly before finalizing.

I can also adjust the tone (more cinematic, more journalistic, more fundraising-focused) or write interview questions to help gather the real material.

The prompt ends without a question, so I'll assume you want a structured synthesis of the design. Tell me if you wanted something else, such as user stories, an architecture diagram, a payments flow spec, or a risk analysis.

## 1. Platform Summary

**Purpose:** A B2B2C cross-border marketplace integration layer connecting marketplace.walmart.com and Walmart's international sites (.ca, .mx, .uk) plus partner marketplaces (JD.com, Rakuten).

**Core modules:**
1. Seller onboarding and catalog sync
2. Order management (OMS)
3. Logistics and fulfillment (FedEx as carrier and channel integrator)
4. Duties, taxes, and landed-cost calculation
5. Payments and payouts (Payoneer, with World First and Tipalti as alternatives)
6. Working capital (Payoneer white-label)
7. Marketing (Walmart Connect)
8. Parcel spend management and billing reconciliation (Green Mountain, DCC)

## 2. Fulfillment Models

| | Model 1: Export Hub | Model 2: Fulfill with Walmart | Model 3: Merch Direct |
|---|---|---|---|
| Inventory location | Seller's warehouse | Split: top SKUs at FedEx FC, the rest with seller | Seller's warehouse only |
| Seller action | Ships each order to a single Export Hub | None for SKUs in the FC; otherwise ships to the FC | Ships directly via FedEx using the provided documents |
| Customs and last mile | FedEx | FedEx | FedEx |
| Key constraints | Entire catalog through **one** hub | Each SKU in **exactly one** location (mutually exclusive) | Seller must receive the invoice, packing slip, and instructions |

**Model 1 order-flow rules:**
- The order is created in FedEx Cross Border **only after** the seller acknowledges the order (it could still be canceled) **and** ships it. FedEx needs the inbound tracking number.
- The platform **intercepts the seller's ship notification** and replaces the domestic tracking number with a **universal FedEx tracking number**. This gives the customer end-to-end visibility rather than updates for only the first leg.

**Model 2 routing logic:**
```
On order placed:
  if SKU.location == FEDEX_FC:
      auto-release to FedEx (no seller action)
  else:
      route to seller -> seller ships to FC -> FedEx clears customs -> last mile
```
The system must enforce SKU-location exclusivity with a validation rule and avoid double-counting inventory.

## 3. Pricing, Duties, and Taxes

- The seller's prices are in CAD, and the shopper pays in CAD. Because **no currency conversion** is needed for customer pricing, duties are also calculated in CAD.
- Shipping and handling are **not** part of the calculated price. The seller sets customer-facing shipping fees, which can be $0.
- Under DDP, the carrier calculates and guarantees duties and taxes, and remits duties to customs.
- The seller decides how much tax to collect. This is a compliance risk to flag with legal.
- The platform receives an **estimated logistics cost** message, which is later trued up to actuals.

## 4. Payments and Payout Flow

**Example:** The item sells for $100 and the referral fee is 10%, so the seller is owed $90 before logistics adjustments.

1. The shopper pays Walmart.ca in CAD.
2. The OMS calculates commission and creates an **accounts payable invoice** for the seller.
3. Walmart funds the Payoneer CAD funding account, daily and automatically.
4. Per the payout calendar (initially biweekly, later spread out), a **payout request** goes to Payoneer.
5. Funds are placed in the **seller escrow account**. Daily funding includes estimated logistics deductions, because funds cannot be withdrawn from escrow.
6. Payoneer pays the seller's wallet in their chosen currency (CAD, USD, CNY, and so on).
7. The carrier sends an aggregate invoice in arrears, biweekly or monthly. The PSM provider (Green Mountain) audits it and uploads it to the DCC, where tracking numbers are linked to rate cards.
8. CBT-Logistics compares actual with estimated cost and **adjusts the next payout** for any variance.

**Improvement:** Get actual package weight from FedEx at the hub scan. This allows accurate charges up front and avoids end-of-cycle adjustments.

**Controls:**

Since the introduction of Tropicana smoothies in 2008, the company has succeeded in strengthening its market presence through a variety of strategies, including extensive television ad campaigns. Its ethical principles are comparable to those of Innocent in terms of protecting the environment. Tropicana's entry, backed by PepsiCo's large budget and distribution network, posed a real threat to Innocent, which had previously dominated the UK smoothie market.

**Innocent's response**

Innocent responded by strengthening its brand and seeking investment rather than competing on advertising spend alone. It continued to emphasise its natural, "no concentrates" recipes, its ethical sourcing and its playful brand identity, while widening its range with products such as kids' smoothies and veg pots. In 2009 it also sold a minority stake (around 20%) to Coca-Cola, which gave it the funding and distribution to expand across Europe and compete with PepsiCo-owned Tropicana. Coca-Cola's share later rose to a majority holding and then full ownership.

**Advantages**

- Access to Coca-Cola's capital, supply chain and distribution allowed Innocent to expand faster and match Tropicana's reach.
- Product diversification reduced reliance on a single product and appealed to new customer groups, such as families.
- Keeping its natural, ethical positioning helped it stay distinct from a large corporate competitor.

**Disadvantages**

- The deal drew criticism from loyal customers, who felt that selling to Coca-Cola contradicted Innocent's ethical, independent image.
- Innocent risked losing control over its values, sourcing and decision-making as Coca-Cola's stake grew.
- The difference between Innocent and Tropicana became less clear, since both were now owned by major soft drink corporations. This weakened Innocent's "small, ethical alternative" appeal.

**Overall evaluation**

Overall, Innocent's reaction was more good than bad for the company. Despite short-term backlash and some damage to its authenticity, the investment secured its financial position, supported international growth and kept it competitive against a well-funded rival. Innocent has remained a market leader, suggesting that most consumers prioritised product quality and brand familiarity over concerns about ownership. However, the response shows a trade-off between commercial growth and maintaining the independent, ethical image on which the brand was built, and this could affect long-term customer loyalty.

query: Big Companies Are Embracing Analytics, But Most Still Don’t Have a Data-Driven Culture by Thomas H. Davenport and Randy Bean For six consecutive years NewVantage Partners has conducted an annual survey on how executives in large corporations view data. This year, results show nearly every firm is investing in some form of analytics, and most are seeing value. But only one-third say they have succeeded in creating a data-driven culture. And many fear disruption by firms better equipped to use AI. Almost four in five respondents said they feared disruption or displacement from firms like those in the fintech sector or firms specializing in big data. The technology judged most disruptive is AI — by far. Seventy-two percent chose it as the disruptive technology with the most impact — far more than cloud computing (13%) or blockchain (7%). For six consecutive years NewVantage Partners has conducted an annual survey on how executives in large corporations view data. Each year the response rate increases, and the reported urgency of making effective use of data increases as well. This year the results are both more encouraging and more worrisome than in the past. Six years ago, the primary focus of questions and answers in the survey was big data, which was relatively new on the business scene. In the 2018 survey, the primary attention has moved to artificial intelligence. AI is now a well-established focus at these large, sophisticated firms. There is both a stronger feeling that big data and AI projects deliver value and a greater concern that established firms will be disrupted by startups. The survey includes senior executives from 57 large corporations. The industry group with the most firms represented in the survey is one of the most data-intensive: financial services. Companies from the life sciences, manufacturing, telecom, and online industries also participated. The actual respondents are changing somewhat from the first surveys: It has always involved a high proportion of C-level executives responsible for data, but this year chief data officers are 56% of the respondents, up from 32% last year. Only 12% of firms in the 2012 survey had even appointed a chief data officer. While AI gets the headlines here and elsewhere in the world, the survey addresses both big data and AI. Terminology comes and goes, but the constant is a data explosion and the need to make sense of it. Big data and AI projects have become virtually indistinguishable, particularly given that machine learning is one of the most popular techniques for dealing with large volumes of fast-moving data. It’s also the case that statistical approaches to AI — deep learning, for example — are increasingly popular. Therefore, we view traditional data analytics, big data, and AI as being on a continuum. Virtually all of the respondents (97%) say they are investing in these types of projects. Perhaps the best news in this survey is that companies continue to believe they are getting value from their big data and AI projects. 73% of respondents said they have already received measurable value from these initiatives. That number is half again higher than in the 2017 survey, which suggests that more value is being achieved as companies grow familiar with the technologies. The types of value received are perhaps consistent with other previous types of technology. Consistent with our view that big data and AI are extensions of analytical capabilities, the most common objectives — and those most likely to achieve success — are “advanced analytics/better decisions.” Thirty-six percent had that as their top priority, and 69% of those had already achieved success with the objective. Better customer service and expense reduction are also common objectives. Just over one-quarter of firms (27%) are pursuing some combination of innovation and disruption, speed to market, or data monetization initiatives. Data monetization programs had the lowest priority and the lowest percentage of success (27%). One of the greatest issues for concern in the survey for large enterprises is the risk of disruption from new entrants. Almost four in five respondents said they feared disruption or displacement from firms like those in the fintech sector or firms specializing in big data. The technology judged most disruptive is AI — by far. Seventy-two percent chose it as the disruptive technology with the most impact — far more than cloud computing (13%) or blockchain (7%). Another important and continuing issue is the slow speed with which these established firms make the shift to a data-driven culture. Virtually all respondents (99%) say their firms are trying to move in that direction, but only about one-third have succeeded at this objective. This gap appears every year in the surveys, and the level of success hasn’t improved much over time. Clearly firms need more-concerted programs to achieve data-related cultural change. Many startups have created data-driven cultures from their beginning, which is a key reason why large, established firms fear disruption from them. One of the approaches that firms have established to deal with data-driven disruption and change is to establish new management roles. However, there is still a lack of clarity about how different data-oriented roles (chief information officer, chief data officer, chief digital officer, chief analytics officer, etc.) relate to each other. With respect to the chief data officer role, there is substantial disagreement about the major responsibilities of the role and what types of backgrounds are appropriate for CDO jobs. Thirty-nine percent say their CDO has primary responsibility for data strategy and results, but 37% assign that responsibility to other C-level executives, and 24% say there is no single point of accountability for it. In terms of backgrounds, 34% of respondents believe the CDO should be a change agent from outside the company, while 32% believe the person should be a company veteran from inside the firm. Role clarity in senior data-related roles is critical for both leading AI/big data projects and accomplishing cultural change. And while all respondents believed it important, the majority of firms still lack an enterprise data strategy. This continuing rise in the importance and challenges of big data is one of the most important features of contemporary economy and society. The survey results over time provide interesting and useful documentation of this revolution. The rise of AI is only exacerbating this trend. The keys to success are to determine how your firm should respond, assign clear responsibilities for data strategy and results, and then move ahead to execute the needed changes in a systematic and effective fashion. 翻译成中文

# 大公司纷纷拥抱数据分析,但多数仍未形成数据驱动的文化

作者:托马斯·H·达文波特(Thomas H. Davenport)、兰迪·比恩(Randy Bean)

NewVantage Partners 已连续六年开展年度调查,了解大型企业的高管如何看待数据。今年的结果显示,几乎所有公司都在投资某种形式的数据分析,而且大多数已看到成效。但只有三分之一的公司表示成功建立了数据驱动的文化,许多公司还担心被更善于运用人工智能的企业颠覆。

近五分之四的受访者表示,他们担心被金融科技领域的公司或专注于大数据的公司颠覆或取代。人工智能被认为是最具颠覆性的技术,而且遥遥领先:72%的受访者选择它作为影响最大的颠覆性技术,远高于云计算(13%)和区块链(7%)。

NewVantage Partners 已连续六年开展年度调查,了解大型企业高管对数据的看法。每年的回复率都在上升,企业对有效利用数据的紧迫感也在增强。今年的结果比以往既更令人鼓舞,也更令人担忧。

六年前,调查的问题与回答主要聚焦大数据,当时它在商界还是新事物。而在 2018 年的调查中,关注重点已转向人工智能。在这些大型、成熟的公司中,人工智能如今已成为稳固的关注焦点。一方面,人们更加确信大数据和人工智能项目能创造价值;另一方面,也更担心老牌企业会被初创公司颠覆。

调查涵盖 57 家大型企业的高级管理人员。参与调查企业最多的行业是数据最密集的行业之一:金融服务业。生命科学、制造、电信和在线行业的公司也参与了调查。实际的受访者与最初几次调查相比有所变化:受访者中一直有很高比例的负责数据的 C 级高管,而今年首席数据官占 56%,去年为 32%。在 2012 年的调查中,设立了首席数据官的公司只有 12%。

虽然人工智能在这里和世界各地都占据着头条,但本调查同时涉及大数据和人工智能。术语来来去去,不变的是数据的爆炸式增长以及理解数据的需要。大数据项目与人工智能项目已几乎无法区分,尤其是因为机器学习是处理海量高速数据最常用的技术之一。同时,基于统计的人工智能方法(例如深度学习)也越来越流行。因此,我们认为传统数据分析、大数据和人工智能处于同一个连续体上。几乎所有受访者(97%)表示正在投资这类项目。

也许调查中最好的消息是,企业仍然相信自己从大数据和人工智能项目中获得了价值。73%的受访者表示已经从这些举措中获得了可衡量的价值,这一比例比 2017 年调查高出一半,说明随着企业对这些技术日益熟悉,正在实现更多价值。

所获得的价值类型也许与以往的技术类似。与我们认为大数据和人工智能是分析能力的延伸这一观点一致,最常见的目标(也是最有可能成功的目标)是"高级分析/更好的决策"。36%的受访者将其作为首要任务,其中 69%已经在这一目标上取得成功。改善客户服务和降低费用也是常见目标。略多于四分之一(27%)的公司在追求创新与颠覆、加快上市速度或数据变现等举措的某种组合。数据变现项目的优先级最低,成功率也最低(27%)。

对大型企业而言,调查中最令人担忧的问题之一是来自新进入者的颠覆风险。近五分之四的受访者表示担心被金融科技领域的公司或专注于大数据的公司颠覆或取代。人工智能被认为是最具颠覆性的技术,而且遥遥领先:72%的受访者选择它作为影响最大的颠覆性技术,远高于云计算(13%)和区块链(7%)。

另一个持续存在的重要问题是,这些老牌企业向数据驱动文化转型的速度缓慢。几乎所有受访者(99%)表示他们的公司正努力朝这个方向前进,但只有约三分之一取得了成功。这一差距每年的调查中都会出现,而且成功率多年来几乎没有改善。显然,企业需要更有力的计划来实现与数据相关的文化变革。许多初创公司从创立之初就建立了数据驱动的文化,这正是大型老牌企业担心被它们颠覆的重要原因。

企业应对数据驱动的颠覆与变革的方法之一,是设立新的管理职位。然而,各类数据相关职位(首席信息官、首席数据官、首席数字官、首席分析官等)之间的关系仍不明确。就首席数据官而言,对于该职位的主要职责以及适合担任者的背景,存在很大分歧。39%的受访者表示由首席数据官主要负责数据战略和成果,但 37%把这一责任交给其他 C 级高管,24%则表示没有单一的责任人。在背景方面,34%的受访者认为首席数据官应是来自公司外部的变革推动者,32%则认为应是公司内部的资深员工。

对于领导人工智能/大数据项目以及实现文化变革而言,高级数据相关职位的角色清晰至关重要。而且,尽管所有受访者都认为企业数据战略很重要,但大多数公司仍然缺乏这样的战略。

大数据的重要性与挑战持续上升,是当代经济和社会最重要的特征之一。历年的调查结果为这场变革提供了有趣而有用的记录。人工智能的兴起只会加剧这一趋势。成功的关键在于:确定贵公司应如何应对,明确数据战略和成果的责任归属,然后系统而有效地推进所需的变革。

Terminology comes and goes, but the constant is a data explosion and the need to make sense of it. Big data and AI projects have become virtually indistinguishable, particularly given that machine learning is one of the most popular techniques for dealing with large volumes of fast-moving data. It’s also the case that statistical approaches to AI — deep learning, for example — are increasingly popular. Therefore, we view traditional data analytics, big data, and AI as being on a continuum. Virtually all of the respondents (97%) say they are investing in these types of projects. Perhaps the best news in this survey is that companies continue to believe they are getting value from their big data and AI projects. 73% of respondents said they have already received measurable value from these initiatives. That number is half again higher than in the 2017 survey, which suggests that more value is being achieved as companies grow familiar with the technologies. The types of value received are perhaps consistent with other previous types of technology. Consistent with our view that big data and AI are extensions of analytical capabilities, the most common objectives — and those most likely to achieve success — are “advanced analytics/better decisions.” Thirty-six percent had that as their top priority, and 69% of those had already achieved success with the objective. Better customer service and expense reduction are also common objectives. Just over one-quarter of firms (27%) are pursuing some combination of innovation and disruption, speed to market, or data monetization initiatives. Data monetization programs had the lowest priority and the lowest percentage of success (27%). One of the greatest issues for concern in the survey for large enterprises is the risk of disruption from new entrants. Almost four in five respondents said they feared disruption or displacement from firms like those in the fintech sector or firms specializing in big data. The technology judged most disruptive is AI — by far. Seventy-two percent chose it as the disruptive technology with the most impact — far more than cloud computing (13%) or blockchain (7%). Another important and continuing issue is the slow speed with which these established firms make the shift to a data-driven culture. Virtually all respondents (99%) say their firms are trying to move in that direction, but only about one-third have succeeded at this objective. This gap appears every year in the surveys, and the level of success hasn’t improved much over time. Clearly firms need more-concerted programs to achieve data-related cultural change. Many startups have created data-driven cultures from their beginning, which is a key reason why large, established firms fear disruption from them. One of the approaches that firms have established to deal with data-driven disruption and change is to establish new management roles. However, there is still a lack of clarity about how different data-oriented roles (chief information officer, chief data officer, chief digital officer, chief analytics officer, etc.) relate to each other. With respect to the chief data officer role, there is substantial disagreement about the major responsibilities of the role and what types of backgrounds are appropriate for CDO jobs. Thirty-nine percent say their CDO has primary responsibility for data strategy and results, but 37% assign that responsibility to other C-level executives, and 24% say there is no single point of accountability for it. In terms of backgrounds, 34% of respondents believe the CDO should be a change agent from outside the company, while 32% believe the person should be a company veteran from inside the firm. Role clarity in senior data-related roles is critical for both leading AI/big data projects and accomplishing cultural change. And while all respondents believed it important, the majority of firms still lack an enterprise data strategy. This continuing rise in the importance and challenges of big data is one of the most important features of contemporary economy and society. The survey results over time provide interesting and useful documentation of this revolution. The rise of AI is only exacerbating this trend. The keys to success are to determine how your firm should respond, assign clear responsibilities for data strategy and results, and then move ahead to execute the needed changes in a systematic and effective fashion.

meta.pupa_reference: 大公司正在采纳数据分析，但大多数仍未形成数据驱动的文化 托马斯·H·达文波特和兰迪·比恩著 六年来，NewVantage Partners连续进行了关于大型企业高管如何看待数据的年度调查。今年的结果显示，几乎每家公司都在某种形式的数据分析上有所投入，大多数公司认为数据分析很有价值。但只有三分之一的公司表示他们成功地创建了一个数据驱动的文化。许多人担心，那些更擅长使用人工智能的公司会对他们造成颠覆。近五分之四的受访者表示，他们担心会被金融科技领域的公司或专注于大数据的公司颠覆或取代。被认为最具颠覆性的技术是人工智能——远远领先。72%的人选择它作为最具影响力的颠覆技术——远远超过云计算（13%）或区块链（7%）。六年来，NewVantage Partners每年都在进行这项调查，每年的响应率都在增加，对有效使用数据的紧迫性也在增加。今年的结果比以往既更令人鼓舞又更令人担忧。 六年前，调查中的主要问题和回答集中在大数据上，这对商业界来说是相对较新的领域。在2018年的调查中，主要的注意力已转移到人工智能上。人工智能现在已经成为这些大型、成熟公司的一个重要焦点。人们越来越觉得大数据和AI项目能够提供价值，并且越来越担心成熟的公司会被初创公司颠覆。 这项调查包括了来自57家大型公司的高级执行官。在调查中代表最多的行业群体之一是最注重数据的：金融服务业。生命科学、制造业、电信和在线行业的公司也参与了调查。实际回应者在从第一次调查至今有所变化：它一直涉及负责数据的C级高管的高比例，但今年的首席数据官占了回应者的56%，而去年是32%。2012年的调查中，只有12%的公司任命了首席数据官。 虽然人工智能在这里和世界其他地方都占据了头条，但调查既包括大数据也包括人工智能。术语来来去去，但不变的是数据爆炸和理解这些数据的需求。大数据和AI项目已经变得几乎无法区分，特别是考虑到机器学习是处理大量快速移动数据的最受欢迎的技术之一。统计方法对于AI也越来越受欢迎——例如深度学习。因此，我们认为传统数据分析、大数据和人工智能处于一个连续体上。几乎所有的受访者（97%）都表示他们正在这些类型的项目上投资。 调查中最好的消息是，公司继续相信他们从大数据和人工智能项目中获得了价值。73%的受访者表示，他们已经从这些计划中获得了可衡量的价值。这个数字比2017年调查中的数字高出了一半，这表明随着公司对技术的熟悉，获得的价值在增加。 获得的价值类型或许与其他以前的技术类型一致。与我们认为大数据和人工智能是分析能力扩展的观点一致，最普遍的目标——也是最有可能成功的目标——是“高级分析/更好的决策”。36%的人将其作为他们的首要任务，其中69%的人已经成功实现了这个目标。更好的客户服务和费用减少也是常见的目标。略超过四分之一的公司（27%）正在追求某种结合创新和颠覆、市场速度或数据货币化计划的目标。数据货币化项目的优先级最低，成功百分比也最低（27%）。 对于大型企业来说，调查中最大的担忧之一是来自新进入者的颠覆风险。近五分之四的受访者表示，他们担心会被金融科技领域的公司或专注于大数据的公司颠覆或取代。被认为最具颠覆性的技术是AI——远远领先。72%的人选择它作为最具影响力的颠覆技术——远远超过云计算（13%）或区块链（7%）。 另一个重要且持续的问题是这些成立公司以多快的速度转型为数据驱动的文化。几乎所有的回应者（99%）都表示他们的公司正试图朝这个方向转型，但是只有大约三分之一成功实现了这个目标。每年的调查中都会出现这个差距，而且随着时间的推移，成功的水平并没有多大提高。显然，公司需要更加集中的项目来实现与数据相关的文化变革。许多初创公司从一开始就创建了数据驱动的文化，这是大型成熟公司害怕被它们颠覆的一个主要原因。 公司建立新的管理角色是处理数据驱动的颠覆和变革的方法之一。然而，不同的数据导向角色（首席信息官、首席数据官、首席数字官、首席分析官等）之间的关系仍然缺乏清晰性。 关于首席数据官角色，对于这个角色的主要职责以及CDO职位适合什么样的背景存在显著分歧。39%的人表示他们的CDO主要负责数据战略和结果，但有37%的人将这一责任分配给其他C级高管，还有24%的人表示没有一个单一的责任点对其负责。在背景方面，34%的回应者认为CDO应该是来自公司外部的变革推动者，而32%的人认为这个人应该是来自公司内部的企业老手。对于高层数据相关角色的角色清晰度对于领导AI/大数据项目和实现文化变革都至关重要。尽管所有的回应者都认为这一点很重要，但大多数公司仍然缺乏一个企业数据战略。 大数据的重要性和挑战的持续上升是当代经济和社会最重要的特征之一。随着时间的推移，调查结果提供了这场革命的有趣和有用的记录。人工智能的崛起只是加剧了这一趋势。成功的关键是确定你的公司应该如何应对，明确分配数据战略和结果的责任，然后着手以系统和有效的方式实施所需的改变。

reference:
Overall the text is understandable, but it has several grammar, word-choice, and style issues. Here are the main corrections, followed by a revised version.

**Main issues**
1. "acceptance of $3,500.00 advance payment" needs an article: "an advance payment of $3,500.00".
2. "Provision of Workshop" needs an article: "the provision of the workshop".
3. "in 14 and 28 January 2024" should be "on 14 and 28 January 2024".
4. "as the training for PCA Staff to be one of supportive nursing assistant team" is unclear and ungrammatical. It should be reworded, e.g. "to help PCA staff become part of a supportive nursing assistant team".
5. "A quotation invitation was arranged" is better as "A quotation exercise was conducted".
6. "The only offer is accepted by user" should read "The only offer was accepted by the user".
7. "approval of quotation has been granted" is better as "approval of the quotation was granted".
8. "had provided a similar workshop to KEC TKOH" is better as "had provided a similar workshop to KEC and TKOH" (or "to TKOH KEC"; clarify which is intended).
9. "Payment Terms Request by Vendor" is awkward; use "Payment Terms Requested by the Vendor".
10. "they requested hospital to arrange" should be "they requested that the hospital arrange".
11. "Advance payment is also applied to all clients" should be "The advance payment requirement applies to all clients."
12. "Order is pending subject to" is redundant; use "The order will be placed subject to…".

**Revised version**

**Remark:** Payment to be settled by bank transfer on or before 8 January 2024.

Dear Roy,

We would like to seek CGM(F)'s approval to accept an advance payment of $3,500.00 for the provision of the "Team Alignment Workshop" for TKOH by Miniu Limited (Miniu).

**Brief Description of the Purchase**
TKOH/NSD will host the "Team Alignment Workshop" on 14 and 28 January 2024. The training will help PCA staff become part of a supportive nursing assistant team and learn skills to communicate more effectively with colleagues and patients.

**Quotation Exercise Conducted by Cluster Procurement**
A quotation invitation was issued on 20 November 2023, and a single bid was received from Miniu. The offer was accepted by the user, and approval of the quotation was granted by HM(P&MM) on 29 November 2023. According to purchase records, Miniu provided a similar workshop to KEC and TKOH in 2023.

**Payment Terms Requested by the Vendor**
Under Miniu's payment terms, the vendor has requested that the hospital arrange an advance payment of $3,500.00 to cover the initial expenses for preparation work. This requirement applies to all of Miniu's clients.

**Approval Sought**
CGM(F)'s approval is sought to accept the advance payment of $3,500.00. The order will be placed once the advance payment is approved.

Supporting documents, including the PR, quotation offer, and approval of quotation, are attached for your reference.

Please check whether "KEC TKOH" should be "KEC and TKOH" or something else, since I assumed the former.

query: I have a business named Shumti and Co, that is an opticians shop with bespoke frames from special brands. We are also able to do lenses for people in 10 minutes, no need to wait for days. What are some strategies that we could implement across social media platforms? and can you give me a business plan that could increase our sales?
reference:
# Shumti and Co: Social Media Strategy & Sales Growth Plan

## Part 1: Positioning

Your two biggest differentiators are **bespoke/specialist frames** and **10-minute lenses**. Everything should reinforce this idea:

> **"Exceptional frames. Ready while you are."**

Most opticians force a choice between quality and convenience. You offer both.

---

## Part 2: Social Media Strategy by Platform

### Instagram (your primary platform)
- **Reels:** Film the 10-minute lens process as a timelapse, with an on-screen timer. This is your most shareable content.
- **Frame spotlights:** Short close-ups of a single frame, with the brand story and who it suits.
- **Customer transformations:** "Walked in with old glasses, left in 10 minutes with these." (Always get written consent.)
- **Stories:** Polls such as "Which frame for this face shape?", new arrivals, and behind-the-scenes content.
- **Highlights:** Organise into Brands, Reviews, How It Works and Location.

### TikTok
- "Trying on frames until we find the one" series
- "POV: you break your glasses and need them today"
- Myth-busting: "Do blue light lenses work?" "Can you really get glasses in 10 minutes?"
- Staff personality content, as people buy from people
- Trending sounds, but tied to your offer

### Facebook
- Local community focus: events, offers and reviews
- Run local geo-targeted ads (see below)
- Join and contribute to local groups (follow their rules on promotion)
- Customer reviews and recommendations

### Google Business Profile (essential, and often overlooked)
- Complete every field, add photos weekly and post updates
- Ask every happy customer for a review
- Use keywords such as "same-day glasses," "designer frames," and "opticians near me"

### YouTube / Shorts
- Repurpose Reels and TikToks
- Longer guides such as "How to choose frames for your face shape"

### Pinterest (optional but valuable)
- Boards for face shapes, seasonal styles and frame trends. Pins last for months and drive traffic.

### LinkedIn (optional)
- Useful only if you pursue corporate eyewear partnerships or staff vision schemes.

---

## Part 3: Content Pillars

| Pillar | Example | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Speed** | 10-minute timer videos | Differentiation |
| **Craft & Brands** | Brand stories, frame details | Premium perception |
| **Education** | Lens types, eye health tips | Trust |
| **Social proof** | Reviews, customer photos | Conversion |
| **People** | Team, shop life | Connection |

**Posting rhythm:** 3-4 Reels/TikToks per week, daily Stories, 1-2 feed posts, and a weekly Google post.

---

## Part 4: Growth Tactics

1. **Branded hashtag:** e.g. #ShumtiIn10 and #ShumtiFrames
2. **Local influencers:** Partner with micro-influencers (2k-30k followers) in fashion, lifestyle and your town. Offer a free pair in exchange for honest content.
3. **User-generated content:** Give a small discount for tagged posts. Make the shop photogenic, with a mirror or backdrop that is "Instagrammable."
4. **Giveaways:** "Win a pair of frames" requiring a follow, a tag and a share. Keep it local and relevant.
5. **Paid ads (start at £5-10/day):**
   - Geo-target a 5-10 mile radius
   - Video ad: "Glasses in 10 minutes"
   - Retarget people who viewed your profile or website
6. **Booking link:** Add an eye-test or appointment link to every bio and post.

---

## Part 5: Business Plan to Increase Sales

### Step 1: Foundations (Month 1)
- Audit your current numbers: average sale, footfall, conversion rate, repeat rate and best sellers
- Set goals, e.g. **+20% revenue in 6 months**
- Set up online booking, Google Business Profile, a simple website, and Meta Pixel/analytics
- Build a professional content bank: photograph every frame and film the 10-minute process

### Step 2: Attract (Months 1-3)
- Launch the social media plan above
- Start paid local ads
- Get 30+ Google reviews
- Contact local businesses, gyms, offices and schools about partnerships

### Step 3: Convert (Months 2-4)
- **Offers to consider:**
  - Second-pair discount (a major revenue driver)
  - Free lens upgrade (e.g. anti-glare) with frame purchase
  - "Broke your glasses? Fixed today" emergency service
- Train staff to suggest add-ons: blue light filters, transition lenses, sunglasses, cases and cleaning kits
- Use a simple style consultation to personalise the experience and justify premium pricing

### Step 4: Retain (Months 3-6)
- Collect emails and phone numbers (with consent)
- Send reminders when an eye test or new pair is due
- Launch a **loyalty scheme** and a **referral reward** (e.g. £10 off for both parties)
- Send new-collection previews to existing customers

### Step 5: Expand Revenue Streams (Months 4-12)
- **Sunglasses** (prescription and non-prescription)
- **Kids' eyewear** (frequent replacement)
- **Corporate/workplace eyewear**
- **Pop-up events** or partnerships with salons, boutiques and cafes
- **Online store or "reserve online, collect in 10 minutes"**
- **Private-label or limited-edition frames**

---

## Part 6: Key Metrics to Track

| Metric | Target |
|---|---|
| Monthly revenue | Steady growth |
| Average transaction value | Increase through add-ons |
| Appointments booked via social | Track weekly |
| Google reviews and rating | 50+ at 4.8+ |
| Cost per new customer | Under 10-15% of average sale |
| Repeat customer rate | Increase quarterly |
| Social engagement and follower growth | Reach and saves matter more than likes |

---

## Part 7: Quick Wins This Week
1. Film a 10-minute lens timelapse and post it as a Reel
2. Update your Google Business Profile with new photos
3. Ask your last 20 customers for a review
4. Add a clear "Glasses in 10 minutes" sign in your window
5. Create a simple second-pair offer

---

## Important Considerations
- **Regulations:** Optical advertising has rules (in the UK, GOC guidelines). Avoid unsubstantiated health claims, and ensure any "10 minutes" claim is accurate and notes any exceptions (e.g. complex prescriptions).
- **Consent:** Always get permission before posting customers.
- **Consistency beats intensity:** A steady schedule matters more than occasional bursts.

---

If you share your **location, budget, target customers, and current social following**, I can create a tailored 90-day content calendar, ad copy, or a pricing and promotions plan.
